title: Configurationally Locked Ridaifen-B Analogs as Potent Ebola Virus Entry Inhibitors.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Ebola virus disease remains a global public health threat due to emerging outbreaks, high mortality rates, and limited treatment options, necessitating the discovery of effective antiviral therapies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study reports the design, synthesis, and evaluation of a series of cyclized ridaifen-B-based inhibitors targeting Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) to disrupt viral entry.
analysis.methods: The authors synthesized and tested cyclized ridaifen-B analogs for antiviral activity against Ebola virus GP-mediated entry, using site-directed mutagenesis to identify inhibitor binding at the GP1/GP2 fusion loop.
analysis.main_results: Several compounds demonstrated nanomolar potency inhibiting Ebola virus GP-mediated entry and submicromolar potency against Marburg virus entry, with favorable in vitro pharmacokinetic parameters prompting in vivo rapid PK testing for hit compound 41.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identifies 1,2-dihydronaphthalene and tetrahydronaphthalene derivatives as promising leads for antifiloviral agents, highlighting their potential as Ebola virus entry inhibitors with binding at the GP fusion loop.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the development of targeted antiviral therapies against Ebola virus, addressing a critical unmet need in outbreak response and treatment options.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to in vitro and preliminary in vivo pharmacokinetic assessments, with no reported efficacy data in animal models or clinical trials, warranting cautious interpretation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates cyclized ridaifen-B analogs as potential Ebola virus entry inhibitors due to the urgent need for effective therapies amid high mortality and limited treatment options. The authors designed, synthesized, and evaluated a series of compounds targeting the Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) to block viral entry, identifying nanomolar potency inhibitors and mapping binding to the GP1/GP2 fusion loop via site-directed mutagenesis. Several compounds also showed submicromolar activity against Marburg virus entry and favorable pharmacokinetic properties, encouraging further in vivo testing. The work highlights 1,2-dihydronaphthalene and tetrahydronaphthalene derivatives as promising antifiloviral leads. While the findings are novel and mechanistically grounded, the evidence is confined to in vitro and preliminary pharmacokinetic studies, lacking efficacy data in animal models or humans, which limits the strength of conclusions.

title: From Zoonotic Spillover to Hemorrhagic Crisis: Molecular Insights and Epidemiology of Ethiopia’s 2025 Marburg Outbreak Amid Preparedness Gaps and Historical Lethality

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines Marburg virus disease (MVD) caused by Marburg virus (MARV) in Ethiopia’s 2025 outbreak, focusing on the zoonotic spillover from Rousettus aegyptiacus, transmission dynamics, and the central question of how molecular determinants and public health responses influenced outbreak containment.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review synthesizes narrative evidence on MARV molecular determinants (GP–NPC1 mediated entry, VP24-driven interferon antagonism, GP-associated endothelial dysfunction) and Ethiopia’s outbreak response, including genomic sequencing and contact tracing, without reporting systematic search methods, databases, or eligibility criteria.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that MARV’s GP–NPC1 mediated entry and VP24-driven interferon antagonism are key virulence determinants, and that Ethiopia’s rapid genomic sequencing and contact tracing (achieving >90% coverage) were critical strengths in the 2025 outbreak response.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights persistent gaps in Ethiopia’s diagnostic capacity, clinical readiness, and access to countermeasures despite strong genomic and coordination capabilities, and notes that transmission occurred amid concurrent cholera and population displacement, complicating control efforts.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review proposes a seven-day containment framework integrating low-cost molecular testing, remdesivir therapy, and VSV-MARV ring vaccination to address diagnostic and therapeutic gaps in resource-limited settings.

analysis.summary_en: This review analyzes Ethiopia’s 2025 Marburg virus disease (MVD) outbreak, tracing the zoonotic spillover from Rousettus aegyptiacus to nine confirmed cases and eight deaths (CFR 89%). It identifies MARV’s GP–NPC1 mediated entry, VP24-driven interferon antagonism, and GP-associated endothelial dysfunction as key virulence determinants. The review praises Ethiopia’s rapid genomic sequencing and >90% contact tracing coverage but underscores persistent weaknesses in diagnostics, clinical readiness, and countermeasure access. Transmission occurred amid cholera and displacement, complicating control. A seven-day containment framework combining low-cost molecular testing, remdesivir, and VSV-MARV ring vaccination is proposed to mitigate future outbreaks in resource-limited settings.

title: Digital Health for Pandemic Preparedness: A Critical Review of Innovations, Equity Gaps, and Governance in Infectious Disease Surveillance

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines digital health innovations for infectious disease surveillance, focusing on equity gaps and governance within pandemic preparedness. The central question concerns the role of digital health technologies in surveillance, detection, forecasting, contact tracing, governance, and equity.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a structured thematic narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature published from January 2010 to March 2025, following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from February 5 to 18, 2025, using keywords covering digital-health technologies, infectious diseases, and public-health functions. Records were deduplicated in EndNote X20 and screened by two blinded reviewers (Cohen κ = 0.81). Empirical studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, and reviews were appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Of 1498 records, 142 studies met inclusion criteria, with 48% rated as high quality. The evidence base is regionally skewed, with 41% from high-income countries and 19% from sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia. No technology was universally superior; AI studies were concentrated in high-income countries, while SMS mHealth studies were concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. Across the included studies, digital health is necessary but not sufficient for pandemic preparedness. Equity, sustainability, and accountability are constituents of effectiveness rather than obstacles.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The evidence base is heavily skewed regionally, with significant underrepresentation from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Recurring barriers include algorithmic bias, fragmented interoperability, donor-dependent sustainability, and slow benefit-sharing of pathogen data with LMICs. The binding constraint is increasingly political and institutional will rather than analytic uncertainty.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priorities should include addressing algorithmic bias, improving interoperability, ensuring donor-independent sustainability, and establishing equitable benefit-sharing mechanisms for pathogen data. Governance frameworks must be strengthened to ensure accountability and political commitment.

analysis.summary_en: This review assesses digital health innovations for infectious disease surveillance, focusing on equity gaps and governance in pandemic preparedness. A thematic narrative review of 142 studies from 2010 to 2025 found that digital health is necessary but not sufficient for preparedness, with no technology universally superior. The evidence base is regionally skewed, with 41% from high-income countries and 19% from sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia. Recurring barriers include algorithmic bias, fragmented interoperability, donor-dependent sustainability, and slow benefit-sharing of pathogen data with LMICs. The binding constraint is political and institutional will rather than analytic uncertainty. Implications include prioritizing equity, sustainability, and accountability in digital health implementation.
